0.title: The Father Who Loves, Sends and Welcomes Home
0.essay:
Jesus taught his friends to begin their prayers with two words: “Our Father”. Christians say them so often that we can forget how astonishing they are. The God who made the galaxies, the holy God before whom angels cover their faces, is to be spoken to as a child speaks to a father who loves him.

The first person of the Trinity

Christians believe in one God in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The study The Trinity explains that great truth, The Person & Work of Christ looks at the Son, and The Holy Spirit at the Spirit. This study stands beside them and looks at the Father: who he is, how he has made himself known, and what it means to be his child.

It is easy to think of the Father as the most distant of the three, the one who stays in heaven while the Son comes near and the Spirit lives within us. Some believers secretly picture him as stern and cold, with Jesus as the kind one who keeps him from being angry. This study hopes to put that picture to rest. Jesus came to show us the Father, and what he showed us is a Father who loves, who sends and who welcomes home.

Where we are going

We begin before the world was made, with the Father and his eternal Son. We trace the rare and lovely glimpses of God as Father in the Old Testament, and see how Jesus opened that name to his disciples. We look at the Father’s plan to save, at adoption into his family, at prayer to him, and at his care and discipline. We stop to speak gently to those for whom “father” is a painful word. And we end at the door of the Father’s house, where a father runs down the road to meet his lost son.

The chapters

The Father and the Son Before All Worlds; The Father in the Old Testament; The Father Who Sent His Son; Adopted: From Slaves to Sons and Daughters; “Abba, Father”: Praying to the Father; The Father’s Care and Discipline; When “Father” Is a Hard Word; and The Running Father and the Father’s House.

For reflection

When you pray, how do you picture the one you are speaking to? Is the Father warm or distant to you, and why do you think that is?

1.title: The Father and the Son Before All Worlds
1.essay:
Before there was a world, before the first star or the first angel, there was a Father who loved his Son. That is the deepest thing the Bible tells us about God, and it is the door into everything else in this study.

Not a title he took at Bethlehem

Many people assume that God became “Father” at Bethlehem, or at creation, as a man becomes a father when his first child is born. Scripture says something far more wonderful. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed, “Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5). A few moments later he spoke of the Father’s love for him “before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24).

Before anything was made, there was the Father and the Son, with the Holy Spirit, sharing glory and love. So God did not become a Father. He is Father, as truly and as eternally as he is holy or almighty. There was never a moment when the Father had no Son, and so never a moment when God was without love. As the study The God Who Needs Nothing shows, God did not make the world because he was lonely. Love was already full and overflowing in him.

Begotten, not made

The church has a word for the Son’s eternal relation to the Father: he is “begotten”. The idea is simple. A man makes a table, but he begets a son. What we make is different from us. What we beget shares our nature. That is why the Nicene Creed, agreed in 325 and enlarged in 381, says that the Son is “begotten, not made”. He is not the first and finest of God’s creatures. He is of the very same being as the Father: God from God, Light from Light.

But there is one great difference. A human father exists before his son. The Father’s begetting of the Son has no beginning and no end: this is what theologians mean by the eternal generation of the Son. The early church often used the picture of the sun and its light: there was never a sun without its shining. Hebrews reaches for the same picture: the Son “is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3). Like every illustration, this one limps (light is not a person), as the study The Trinity warns. But it helps. The Son is eternally from the Father, eternally with the Father, and eternally equal to the Father.

Jesus himself puts it this way: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26). The Father eternally gives; the Son eternally receives; and what is given is nothing less than the life of God. As the Westminster Confession sums it up, the Father is of none, the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Spirit eternally proceeds from both.

Not a senior God

Here we must be careful. In human families, “father” and “son” suggest older and younger, greater and lesser. It is not so in God. There is one God, not a senior God and a junior one. Jesus says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and the Father’s purpose is “that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23).

What then of Jesus’ words, “the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28)? He spoke them as the Son made man, on the night of his arrest. In taking our nature and a servant’s place, he freely put himself under the Father to do the work of our salvation. The words speak of his mission, not of a lower rank in his being.

Christians who agree on all of this still discuss one further question. Some respected evangelical teachers, among them Wayne Grudem and Bruce Ware, hold that the Son, while fully equal to the Father in being, eternally submits to the Father’s authority, and that this pattern lies behind the incarnation; they firmly reject the error that the Son is a creature. Others, with the historic creeds and the classical Reformed tradition, answer that there is an eternal order in God (the Father begets and sends; the Son is begotten and sent), but that the one God has one will and one authority, so that obedience belongs to the Son as the incarnate Mediator.

This commentary’s view: the persons are distinguished by their eternal relations, and the Son is eternally begotten of the Father. His submission belongs to the work of salvation he freely undertook as Mediator, not to any subordination of his being. The Father sends because he is the Father; the Son comes because he is the Son. But the Son’s coming was his own glad love, not a lesser god doing as he was told.

No God behind the back of Jesus

Why does this matter? Because when we look at Jesus, we see the Father truly. “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). If the Son were a lesser being, there might be a colder God hidden behind him. But the Son is the exact imprint of the Father. There is no other God behind the back of Jesus. The Father is as gentle as the Son who touched lepers, and as holy as the Son who cleared the temple.

And it means that the love the gospel brings us into is the oldest love there is. Jesus prayed “that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17:26). The gospel does not offer us a new and untested love. It welcomes us into a love that never had a beginning and will never have an end.

An example

A long-time Christian admitted to her home group that she had always pictured Jesus as kind and the Father as stern, watching from a distance with folded arms. As they read John 14:9 together, she fell silent, then said, “So the Father has always looked at me the way Jesus looked at the people he healed.” She began to come to the Father in prayer, and to expect a welcome.

For reflection

What difference does it make that God has always been Father, and did not become one at creation or at Bethlehem? How would you explain “begotten, not made” to a friend? Why is it a comfort that there is no other God hidden behind Jesus? What does it mean to you to be drawn into a love that had no beginning?

2.title: The Father in the Old Testament
2.essay:
Read the Old Testament looking for God as “Father” and you may be surprised how seldom you find the name. It appears only a handful of times, like a few bright stars in a dark sky. But when it shines, it shines with startling tenderness, and it points forward to the One who would open the name to us.

“Israel is my firstborn son”

The first great use comes at the exodus. God sends Moses to Pharaoh with a message: “Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son, and I say to you, ‘Let my son go that he may serve me’” (Exodus 4:22–23). To Pharaoh, Israel was a nation of slaves. To God, Israel was his son, and not just any son but the firstborn, the child of honour and the heir. The exodus is a father coming for his child.

In the wilderness the LORD “carried you, as a man carries his son” (Deuteronomy 1:31). And when they turned away, his rebuke was a father’s grief: “Do you thus repay the LORD, you foolish and senseless people? Is not he your father, who created you, who made you and established you?” (Deuteronomy 32:6).

The nations around Israel told stories of gods who fathered children, and Egypt called its king a son of the sun god. The God of Israel is nothing like that. He is Father as the one who created his people, redeemed them from slavery and bound them to himself in covenant love.

A father’s compassion

David sang: “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:13–14). God knows how weak we are, and his compassion bends down to our size.

God also promised David’s royal son, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Samuel 7:14). Solomon and the kings after him only partly fitted those words. Hebrews tells us who fits them fully: the Father’s own eternal Son (Hebrews 1:5).

The father who taught his son to walk

Perhaps the most moving picture of all is in Hosea. “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1). Then comes the heartbreak: “The more they were called, the more they went away” (Hosea 11:2). Yet God remembers: “it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms, but they did not know that I healed them. I led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love … and I bent down to them and fed them” (Hosea 11:3–4).

Picture a father on his knees on the kitchen floor, holding a wobbling child by both arms as the little feet take their first steps. That is how the holy God describes himself. And when Israel’s rebellion deserves judgment, the Father’s heart cries out: “How can I give you up, O Ephraim? … My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender” (Hosea 11:8).

Matthew applies Hosea’s words to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:15). Israel was a son who kept walking away; Jesus is the true Son who walked the same road and never turned aside.

The prophets’ cry

Centuries later, with Jerusalem in ruins, Isaiah prays a prayer that is almost a sob: “For you are our Father, though Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name” (Isaiah 63:16). Then: “But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter” (Isaiah 64:8). The study Pictures of God looks at that potter more closely.

Jeremiah gives us one of the most surprising sentences in the Old Testament. God says, “I thought you would call me, My Father, and would not turn from following me” (Jeremiah 3:19). Think of that. The LORD of hosts longed to be called Father by his people. And later he says of wayward Ephraim, “Is Ephraim my dear son? Is he my darling child? … Therefore my heart yearns for him” (Jeremiah 31:20).

That fatherhood also carries a claim. Through Malachi, the last of the prophets, God asks, “If then I am a father, where is my honor?” (Malachi 1:6). Careless worship is a son treating his father with contempt.

Why so rare, and how Jesus opened it

Why is the name so rare before Jesus? Perhaps partly to guard Israel from confusing the LORD with the fertility gods of the nations. Partly because God is usually Father to the nation as a whole; individual believers seldom call him “my Father” in prayer. But the deepest reason is that the name was waiting for the Son. The fullness of God’s fatherhood could not be shown until the eternal Son came among us.

And when he came, the word was everywhere on his lips. At twelve years old he said, “Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?” (Luke 2:49). In John’s Gospel alone the name comes more than a hundred times. He taught his disciples to say “Our Father”. And on the morning of his resurrection he sent this message: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). He did not merely use a warmer word for God. He brought his people inside his own relationship with the Father.

There is even a hint of this in the wilderness: “the angel of his presence saved them … he lifted them up and carried them” (Isaiah 63:9). This commentary reads the angel of the LORD as the Son appearing before his incarnation. Even in the desert, it seems, the Father was sending his Son to carry his children home.

An example

A retired schoolteacher read through the Old Testament underlining every place where God is called Father. She found very few. Then she reached the Gospels and found the word on almost every page. “It was like a long, dim corridor,” she said, “and then someone opened the door at the end.”

For reflection

What do Exodus 4 and Hosea 11 tell you about the kind of Father God is? How does it strike you that God longed to be called “My Father” (Jeremiah 3:19)? Why do you think the name waited for the coming of the Son? What did Jesus give his disciples when he said “my Father and your Father”?

3.title: The Father Who Sent His Son
3.essay:
Many people carry a picture of salvation that goes something like this: an angry God in heaven, ready to destroy us, and a gentle Jesus who steps between and pleads with him until he gives way. It is a moving picture. It is also wrong, and it robs us of the Father’s love.

He chose us in love

Paul begins Ephesians with a burst of praise: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:3–4). Salvation did not begin when you first believed, or even at the cross, but in the heart of the Father before there was a world.

And notice the words that follow: “In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 1:4–5). Election is sometimes spoken of as a cold decree. Paul says it was “in love”, and that its goal was a family: “adoption to himself”. The Father did not choose servants to run his errands. He chose children to share his home. The studies The Trinity and The Doctrines of Grace say more about the Father’s plan and about election. Here we simply notice where it all starts: in the Father’s love.

He gave his only Son

The best-known verse in the Bible tells us who sent the Saviour: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). John says it again in his letter: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10).

“Propitiation” is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin. That anger is real; the Bible never makes light of it. But see who provides the sacrifice. Not us, bringing a gift to calm an angry deity. The Father himself, out of love, provides what his own justice requires. Calvin, following Augustine, put it like this: God did not begin to love us because Christ reconciled us; he loved us already, and so he sent his Son to reconcile us. The cross does not buy the Father’s love. It is the Father’s love in action.

Paul measures that love by the size of the gift: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). The words echo the moment when Abraham was told, “you have not withheld your son, your only son” (Genesis 22:12). On Mount Moriah a ram was provided and Isaac went home. On Calvary there was no substitute for the Substitute. We must not imagine the Father suffering as we suffer; Scripture does not speak that way. But it does ask us to measure his love by the gift he gave.

He gave a people to his Son

Jesus speaks of believers as a gift from his Father to him. “All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). His mission is to keep that gift safe: “this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39). In his great prayer he says to the Father, “Yours they were, and you gave them to me” (John 17:6).

Think of it. Before you ever thought of God, the Father gave you to his Son as a love gift, and the Son promised to lose none of it. And “no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:29). Your safety rests on the love of the Father for the Son and the love of the Son for the Father.

Not a reluctant Father

Jesus himself sets aside the picture of a kind Son and a reluctant Father. He told his disciples that they would pray in his name, and added, “I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf; for the Father himself loves you” (John 16:26–27). Christ does pray for us. He “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25), and he is our “advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1). But his prayers are not the begging of a friend before an unwilling judge. They are the Father’s own appointed way of blessing us. The Son never has to change the Father’s mind about you.

And he loved us before we cleaned ourselves up: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). He loved us at our worst.

The cost of the gift

In the Gospels Jesus addresses God in prayer as “Father”, with one exception. On the cross, carrying our sin, he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). For those hours the Son who had always said “Father” spoke as one forsaken. Then, at the very end, the word came back: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46).

He lost the comfort of that name so that we would never lose it. Stuart Townend’s hymn begins, “How deep the Father’s love for us, how vast beyond all measure.” The cross is the measure. The Father who did not spare his Son will never spare any good thing his children need.

An example

A young man grew up believing that Jesus loved him but that the Father only tolerated him for Jesus’ sake. A friend asked him to read John 16:27 aloud. He read it, stopped, and read it again: “the Father himself loves you.” “I have never seen that verse,” he said. He had seen it many times. He had just never believed it was about him.

For reflection

Have you ever pictured Jesus persuading a reluctant Father to accept you? Where did that picture come from? What does it mean that the Father chose you “in love” and gave you to his Son? How does Romans 8:32 speak to the needs you are anxious about? What does Jesus’ cry from the cross tell you about the price of calling God “Father”?

4.title: Adopted: From Slaves to Sons and Daughters
4.essay:
Justification is the courtroom: the Judge declares us righteous for Christ’s sake. Adoption is the family room: the Father takes us home. J. I. Packer argued that adoption is the highest privilege the gospel gives, higher even than justification, because it is one thing to be acquitted by a judge and another to be embraced by a father.

No longer a slave

Paul tells the story of salvation as a move from slavery to sonship. Before Christ we were like an heir who is still a child, “no different from a slave” (Galatians 4:1), held under the rules of a world in bondage. “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’ So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God” (Galatians 4:4–7).

The Father sent twice. He sent his Son into the world to buy us out of slavery, and he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts to teach us to say “Father”. Redemption and adoption belong together. God does not merely set us free. He brings us into his family.

Paul’s readers knew what slavery was. A slave did not belong to the family, however long he served. Jesus put it simply: “The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever” (John 8:35).

What adoption meant in Rome

The Christians in Galatia and Rome lived under Roman law, where adoption was a serious and well-known practice. It was often the adoption of an older boy or a grown man, chosen on purpose to carry on a family. The adopted son passed fully under the authority and care of his new father, took the family name and became an heir with the same rights as a son born into the house. The most famous case was Octavian, later the emperor Augustus, who was adopted in the will of Julius Caesar and so became heir to Caesar’s name and fortune.

Paul’s readers heard in “adoption”: deliberately chosen, given a new name, made an heir. That is what God has done for us.

Notice too that Paul says “sons”. In that world it was usually sons who inherited. Paul is not leaving women out; he is giving every believer, male and female, the full standing of the heir. The Lord says, “you shall be sons and daughters to me” (2 Corinthians 6:18). In Christ there are no second-class children.

Heirs of God

“For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God … and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:14, 17). Read that slowly. Fellow heirs with Christ. Whatever the Father gives his eternal Son, he shares with those who are in him. Jesus is “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29), and “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11).

The inheritance is “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). Above all it is God himself. The heir of a great house inherits the estate; the children of God inherit the Father.

The Spirit of adoption

Adoption is not only a legal fact recorded in heaven. It is also a living experience in the heart. “You did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’ The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:15–16). The study The Holy Spirit looks more closely at this inward witness. Here it is enough to say that the Spirit does not only tell us about the family. He gives us the family voice.

“And so we are”

John could hardly contain himself: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). Those last four words matter. It is not a polite title or a pious way of speaking. It is true. You are his child.

When you feel unworthy

What changes when we fail, and what does not? Our feelings change. Our sense of closeness can grow dim. Sin grieves the Father, and he will deal with it as a father does, which the next units explore. We need to confess, and we have “an advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1).

But our status does not change. Adoption is not probation. You were not adopted because you were worthy, so you cannot be un-adopted for being unworthy. The Father chose you “in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6), and his love for you rests on his love for his Son. A child who breaks a window is still a child of the house; he is not sent back to the orphanage. The feeling of unworthiness is true, but beside the point. Grace was never about worth.

An example

A couple adopted a seven-year-old boy who had lived in several foster homes. For months he hid food under his bed: biscuits, bread rolls, apples. He was sure the meals would stop. His new father never scolded him. Every evening he simply took the boy to the kitchen and showed him the full cupboards. “This is your house,” he would say. “There will be breakfast tomorrow.” It took nearly a year before the hoarding stopped. Many Christians live like that boy, quietly guarding themselves against the day the Father changes his mind. He will not.

For reflection

What is the difference between being forgiven and being adopted? How does the Roman background help you see what God has done? What does it mean to you to be a “fellow heir” with Christ? In what ways do you still live like a slave or an orphan, and what truth would help you live as a child of the house?

5.title: “Abba, Father”: Praying to the Father
5.essay:
Jesus could have taught his followers to begin their prayers with many grand titles: Almighty, Most High, King of the ages. All of them are true. Instead he gave them two simple words: “Our Father”. Prayer, for a Christian, is first of all a child speaking to a father.

Abba

In the garden of Gethsemane, with the cross only hours away, Jesus fell to the ground and prayed, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36). Mark keeps the very word Jesus used. Abba is Aramaic, the everyday family word for “father”. Small children used it, but so did grown sons and daughters. It is sometimes said to mean “Daddy”, which is not quite right. It is warm and close, and also respectful: the word of a child who loves, trusts and honours his father.

Here is the wonder. That word, the Son’s own word for his Father, is now in our mouths. “God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Galatians 4:6). “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). When a Christian, weary and half-believing, whispers “Father” in the dark, it is the Spirit of the Son praying in him, and the Father hears the voice of his beloved Son.

Our Father in heaven

The Lord’s Prayer begins, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9). The study Prayer walks through it line by line. Here notice just the opening. “Our” reminds us that we never pray as only children; we belong to a family. “Father” gives us confidence. “In heaven” gives us reverence: our Father is not a man we can manage, but the Lord of all, with all power to help.

The prayer begins with the Father’s name, kingdom and will, for children who love their father care about his honour. Then it turns to bread, forgiveness and protection. A father does not think his children’s daily needs are too small to bring to him. If bread matters to you, it matters to him.

How much more

Jesus reasons from the lesser to the greater: “What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:11–13).

Even sinful fathers usually want to give their children good things. Notice the gift Jesus names in Luke: the Holy Spirit himself. The Father’s best gift is not a thing but his own presence.

Your Father knows

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus turns the fatherhood of God against our anxiety. “Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?” (Matthew 6:26). The lilies do not toil, yet they are dressed more finely than Solomon. So “do not be anxious … your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:31–33).

Elsewhere he says that not one sparrow falls “apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29). The study Contentment & Anxiety works this out more fully. But see the logic: the cure for worry is not to care less about our needs, but to remember whose children we are.

If the Father already knows, why pray? “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8). Prayer is not giving God information he lacks, or wearing him down until he gives in. It is a child bringing everything to his father because that is what children do. And the asking itself draws us close.

Through the Son, by the Spirit

Christian prayer has a shape: to the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit. “For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). Jesus said, “whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16:23). Praying “in Jesus’ name” is not a magic phrase tacked on to the end. It means coming on his merit, not ours, as people who belong to him and want what he wants. And when we do not know how to pray, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). It is right to pray to the Son and the Spirit too (Acts 7:59), but the usual pattern of Scripture is this: through the Son, by the Spirit, to the Father.

Not my will

Go back to Gethsemane. “Abba” was not only a word of closeness. It was the word Jesus used as he gave up his own will. A child who trusts his father can hear “no” or “not yet” without concluding that he is unloved. The Father said no to his Son that night, and through that no came the salvation of the world.

An example

A nurse on long night shifts was too tired for her old prayer times, felt guilty and began to avoid prayer altogether. An older friend suggested she begin each shift by simply saying, “Father, here I am,” and then speak to him briefly about each patient as she went from bed to bed. Her prayers were short, but they were constant. “I used to think of prayer as an appointment,” she said. “Now it feels more like walking beside my dad.”

For reflection

What does it mean to you that the Spirit puts the Son’s own word, “Abba”, in your mouth? Which of your daily needs have you thought too small to bring to the Father? How does “your heavenly Father knows” speak to your worries this week? Is there a “no” or “not yet” you need to bring to him with “not what I will, but what you will”?

6.title: The Father’s Care and Discipline
6.essay:
If God is our Father, why does life still hurt so much? Why do his children lose jobs, bury husbands, battle illness and wait years for answers? Scripture answers with a surprising word from the vocabulary of love: discipline.

A Father who provides

First, remember how much the Father gives. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). Every meal, every friendship, every morning of health is a gift from his hand. His children do not live in a world where he has stopped caring. They live in a world full of his kindness, even when some days are dark.

Discipline is a family word

Hebrews was written to Christians under pressure, tempted to give up. The writer quotes Proverbs: “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:5–6; compare Proverbs 3:11–12). Then he draws the conclusion: “It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons” (Hebrews 12:7).

The word “discipline” here is a family word. It means training, education and upbringing, not only correction. It is what a good father does in raising a child. Proverbs says the LORD reproves “as a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:12). Delight is the root of it.

Hebrews compares the Father with our earthly fathers: “they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). Human fathers often got it wrong: too harsh, too lenient, too much about their own frustration. The Father never does. His discipline is always wise and measured, and it has a goal: that we may become like him, and so truly happy.

Discipline, not punishment

This is the heart of the matter. For a Christian, suffering is never punishment in the sense of paying for sin. That payment has been made. Christ bore the penalty of our sins on the cross, and “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The Father will never make you pay twice for what his Son has already paid.

Punishment looks backwards: it gives the offender what his offence deserves. Discipline looks forwards: it trains a child for what he can become. A judge punishes; a father disciplines. Because of the cross, God relates to believers as Father, not as Judge. That is why John can say, “There is no fear in love … For fear has to do with punishment” (1 John 4:18).

Suffering is not proof that he is angry

Christians in pain often ask, “What have I done to deserve this?” Sometimes troubles do follow our sins, and the Father uses them to bring us back. But not every trouble is a correction for a particular sin. When the disciples asked whose sin had caused a man’s blindness, Jesus answered, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him” (John 9:3). Job did not suffer because he was wicked; God himself called him “blameless and upright” (Job 1:8).

Some hardship prunes us, some strengthens our faith, and some is the shared grief of a fallen world. All of it is in the Father’s hand. And his heart is not cold while he allows it: “he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men” (Lamentations 3:33). The Father who allows his child to suffer is the Father who remembers “that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). He knows exactly how much we can carry.

A word of care: God’s discipline is never a reason to put up with abuse from another person. If someone is harming you, that is not the Father’s training to be quietly endured. Get to safety and tell someone who can help.

The Son who suffered

If you doubt that a loved child can suffer, look at Jesus. “Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). He was never disciplined for sin, for he had none. But the beloved Son, in whom the Father was well pleased, walked the hardest road any son has ever walked. The most loved Son suffered most. Suffering, then, can never prove that you are unloved.

And he went before us. Hebrews tells us to look “to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). The Father is bringing “many sons to glory” (Hebrews 2:10), and the road home passes through the same country his Son crossed first.

Two ways to get it wrong

Hebrews warns against two errors. One is to “regard lightly” the Father’s discipline: to shrug, harden ourselves and learn nothing. The other is to “be weary”, to faint and lose heart, as though God had turned against us. The way between is to receive hard things as from a Father’s hand: to ask what he may be teaching us, to trust him where we cannot see, and to wait for the promise: “later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11).

An example

A businessman watched the firm he had built for twenty years collapse, and lay awake for months asking, “What is God punishing me for?” His pastor told him gently that Christ had already taken every punishment he deserved, and suggested a different question: “What is my Father doing with me?” Over the next year he found that he had been far more proud and anxious than he knew, and far more loved. He did not get the firm back. He said later that he had gained a Father he had only known by name.

For reflection

What is the difference between discipline and punishment, and why does it matter? Have you ever read a hard time as proof that God was angry with you? How does the suffering of Jesus, the beloved Son, help you? Which do you tend towards, shrugging off God’s training or fainting under it?

7.title: When “Father” Is a Hard Word
7.essay:
For some readers, every page of this study so far has been hard. The word “father” does not bring to mind a warm hand or a safe lap. It brings back a slammed door, an empty chair, a raised voice, a smell of drink, or something far worse. If that is you, this unit is written for you, slowly and gently.

You are not the only one

Scripture is not written only for people with happy childhoods. David wrote, “For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in” (Psalm 27:10). God put those words in the Bible for people who have been left. Another psalm says, “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:5–6). Hosea ends with Israel turning back to God and saying, “In you the orphan finds mercy” (Hosea 14:3).

The God of the Bible has a particular care for the fatherless. He notices the child no one came for. You are not an awkward exception to the message of God’s fatherhood. You are close to the centre of his concern.

The original, not the copy

Our minds work from the people we know. If a father was absent, we expect God to be absent; if he was harsh, we flinch before God. We take the man we knew and enlarge him to the size of the sky.

Scripture runs the other way. Paul writes, “I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” (Ephesians 3:14–15). In Greek the word for “father” (patēr) and the word for “family” (patria) are related; every fatherhood in creation takes its name from him. God is not a copy of your father, enlarged. He is the original, and every human father is a copy: some faithful, some badly smudged, some torn almost beyond recognition. When your father failed you, he did not show you what God is like. He showed you, painfully, what God is not.

So where your father was absent, the Father says, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). Where your father was harsh, the Father “shows compassion to his children” (Psalm 103:13). Where your father was unpredictable, the Father is the one “with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). Where your father crushed what was fragile in you, the Father’s Son is the one who will not break “a bruised reed” (Isaiah 42:3). And if you want to know what the Father’s face looks like, look at Jesus: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). He took children in his arms and touched the untouchable.

A small detail in Mark

Jesus promises that whoever has left “house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands” for his sake will receive a hundredfold “now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands” (Mark 10:29–30). Look closely: fathers are in the first list but not in the second. Many have noticed that in the family of God believers receive many brothers, sisters and mothers, but only one Father. Godly older men in the church can show real fatherly kindness, and they should. But the Father’s place belongs to God alone, and he will not leave it empty.

Honest about the hurt

Knowing God as Father does not mean pretending your father was better than he was. The psalms give us words for lament, and it is right to name a wrong as a wrong. Forgiveness, when you come to it, means giving up the right to pay back; it does not mean saying the harm did not matter, and it does not mean you must trust someone who is not safe. The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation explains the difference, and Shame speaks to those who carry shame that others put on them.

Safety first, and help today

If anyone is abusing you now, at home or anywhere else, your first step is to get safe. Tell a trusted person, contact the police or the proper authorities, and report it. A church should help you do this and report it too; it should never ask you to keep quiet or to stay in danger. If the past is pressing on you so heavily that you have thought of ending your life, please do not wait: today, call the emergency services or a crisis line, or go to someone you trust and tell them.

Healing from a hard childhood usually takes time. Ask your pastor to connect you with a biblical counsellor, through your church or an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the United States or Biblical Counselling UK. A good counsellor will open God’s Word with you, which is sufficient for the care of the soul, and will ask you to see your doctor as well where sleep, anxiety or low mood are part of the picture. Medical treatment is no failure of faith. The study Biblical Counseling says more about how such help works.

Learning the word slowly

Some people find they cannot yet pray “Father” without tensing. That is all right. Begin where Scripture lets you begin. Pray “Father of the fatherless”. Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly, a phrase at a time. Read Luke 15 and look at the father in that story. Keep using the word, trusting that the Spirit who cries “Abba” in you knows the way home.

An example

A woman in her forties had grown up with a father who drank and raged. As a Christian she prayed to “Lord” and “Jesus”, but never to “Father”. With her counsellor she read Psalm 27:10 and Ephesians 3:14–15 many times over several months. One evening, praying for her teenage son, she heard herself say, “Father, please look after him.” She stopped, surprised, and cried. The word had not lost all its pain, but it had begun to belong to someone else.

For reflection

How has your own father, present or absent, shaped the way you think of God? Which of the Father’s qualities in this unit do you most need to believe? What step towards help or safety might you need to take this week? How might you show fatherly or motherly care to someone in your church who has never known it?

8.title: The Running Father and the Father’s House
8.essay:
Jesus told many stories, but none has been loved more than this one. We usually call it the parable of the prodigal son. It might better be called the parable of the running father, for it is the clearest picture Jesus ever painted of his Father, and it ends with a door thrown open and a feast.

Why Jesus told it

“Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2). So Jesus told three stories of lost things, a sheep, a coin and a son, each ending in joy in heaven over “one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7).

The younger son

“There was a man who had two sons” (Luke 15:11). The younger asks for his share of the property now. In a village of that time this was shocking: it treated the father’s wealth as worth more than the father. He takes it to “a far country” and squanders it. A Jewish boy ends up feeding pigs, and longing for their food.

Then “he came to himself” (Luke 15:17). He rehearses a speech: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:18–19). He hopes for a job, not a family.

The running father

“But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). He had been watching the road. He ran. Kenneth Bailey and others who have studied village life in the Middle East have pointed out that a respected older man did not run; to do so he would have to hitch up his robe and lose his dignity in front of everyone. This father took the shame of the moment on himself, and reached his son before the village could.

The son begins his speech (Luke 15:21), but the line about the hired servant never comes. The father has already turned to the servants: “Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet” (Luke 15:22). The best robe for honour, a ring that likely signified authority in the household, shoes on feet that had walked home bare, probably because servants commonly went barefoot and sons did not. And a feast: “For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found” (Luke 15:24). This is the Father whom Jesus came to show us: not one who waits with folded arms for a full apology, but one who runs.

The elder son

The older son hears the music and refuses to go in. “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat” (Luke 15:29). He had stayed at home, but with a servant’s heart, keeping a ledger. And once again the father goes out: “His father came out and entreated him” (Luke 15:28). He says, “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31).

Timothy Keller often pointed out that this is a story of two lost sons: the younger lost through his badness and the elder through his goodness, both wanting the father’s things rather than the father, and that the story lacks a true elder brother who would go to the far country at his own cost to bring the lost one home. The story ends without telling us whether the older son went in, because the door was still open to the grumbling Pharisees, as it is to every proud and dutiful heart.

The true Elder Brother

What the elder brother in the story would not do, Jesus did. The eternal Son left his Father’s side and came to our far country. He was treated as the lost son: stripped, shamed, cast out, crying “My God, my God”. He went into the darkness so that the Father could say over us, “this my son was dead, and is alive again” (Luke 15:24). Our welcome home cost him his life, and he gave it gladly.

The Father’s house

So the story of God the Father ends where every child longs for a story to end: at home. “Let not your hearts be troubled … In my Father’s house are many rooms … I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also” (John 14:1–3).

The last pages of the Bible open that house to us. A voice from the throne says, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). And then the promise that gathers up this whole study: “The one who conquers will have this heritage, and I will be his God and he will be my son” (Revelation 21:7).

Think of where we began: a Father and a Son, loving one another before the world was made. Think of where it ends: that same Father, surrounded by a great family of sons and daughters from every nation, all brought home by that same Son, all crying “Abba” by that same Spirit. Jesus prayed that we would be with him “to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24). The love that had no beginning will have no end, and we will be inside it.

No one comes to the Father except through the Son (John 14:6). But everyone who comes through the Son will find the Father already running down the road.

An example

A man in his fifties walked into a church service for the first time in thirty years and sat at the back. An elderly deacon who had known him as a boy recognised him across the room, and made his way to the back as fast as his stick allowed. He did not say, “Where have you been?” He said, “You’re home,” and held on to him. The man said afterwards that he had expected a lecture, and had met a picture of the Father.

For reflection

Are you more like the younger son or the elder son? What would it mean to want the Father himself, not only his gifts? How does it move you that Jesus became the true Elder Brother who came to bring you home? When you think of the Father’s house, what are you most looking forward to?
